claims.text: The initial material consists of tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions embedded in a copper matrix.
Conventionally processed tungsten surfaces in the initial composite are bare and unmodified.
A thin nickel coating will be applied to tungsten particles before copper infusion and spark-plasma sintering.
The nickel coating will promote formation of a graded interfacial alloy layer at the W–Cu boundary during sintering.
Nickel will react with copper during sintering.
The reaction will produce a localized intermetallic compound or solid solution.
The nickel-derived interfacial phase will improve wetting between tungsten and copper.
Improved wetting will suppress interfacial void formation.
The nickel-derived interface will strengthen bonding between tungsten and copper.
Reduced void formation and stronger interfacial bonding will enhance thermal conductivity.
Reduced void formation and stronger interfacial bonding will maintain mechanical durability under demanding conditions.
Nickel-coated W–Cu composites will have lower interfacial void content than composites made using the vapor-coated tungsten-powder baseline.
Nickel-coated W–Cu composites will have lower thermal interface resistance than the vapor-coated tungsten-powder baseline.
Nickel-coated W–Cu composites will have greater tensile strength than the vapor-coated tungsten-powder baseline.
Nickel-coated W–Cu composites will have greater fatigue resistance than the vapor-coated tungsten-powder baseline.
The named baseline uses vapor-coated tungsten powders and achieves near-perfect W–Cu contact without a reactive interlayer.
Processing will occur below tungsten's melting point of approximately 3422 °C and copper's boiling point of approximately 2562 °C.
The intervention is applicable to spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu composites intended for fusion-reactor heat-transfer joints.
Performance will be assessed under thermal cycling and simulated irradiation.

contradictions.description: The claimed comparison baseline is a composite made from vapor-coated tungsten powders, but the experimental control is described only as tungsten without the nickel coating. Unless that control is explicitly fabricated by the named vapor-coating process, the experiment does not test the stated baseline comparison.
The hypothesis predicts reduced thermal interface resistance, whereas the experiment specifies bulk thermal-conductivity measurements rather than a direct interface-resistance measurement.
